hero.headline: Palm Beach County projects receive $30 million in state budget wins, but some priorities vetoed
hero.teaser: Tri-Rail received $60 million to avoid shutting down in July, while Palm Beach County secured funding for infrastructure upgrades including water treatment and drainage repairs.
hero.body:
Palm Beach County secured over $30 million in funding through Florida's 2026-2027 state budget, representing 75 percent of the money local officials requested, according to Florida State Senator Mack Bernard. The approval came after Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed nearly $1.6 billion in proposed state spending. Despite the governor's significant use of his veto power, major transportation and infrastructure projects in the county moved forward with state support.

The most significant victory was $60 million in funding for Tri-Rail, the commuter rail system serving Palm Beach, Broward, and Miami-Dade counties. Without this state investment, Tri-Rail faced the risk of shutting down in July. The funding provides critical transportation infrastructure for residents commuting between the three counties for work and school. Beyond Tri-Rail, Palm Beach County secured $1.5 million for the new Riviera Beach water treatment plant, $2 million for drainage repairs on Australian Avenue between 45th Street and Palm Beach Lakes as part of a larger $65 million project, and $3 million for traffic safety improvements on Okeechobee Boulevard. The Australian Avenue project had previously been vetoed for $800,000 in an earlier budget cycle. Two social service organizations also received support: $1.5 million went to Arc of the Palm Beaches for a special needs shelter in West Palm Beach, and $1.5 million went to the Teen Readiness Center at the Boys & Girls Club.

However, the governor's veto pen struck down several Palm Beach County priorities. The vetoed projects included $2 million for water treatment plant expansions, $900,000 for road improvements and beautification in South Bay, $125,000 for Ocean Inlet beach access improvements, and $200,000 for repairs and operations at Delray Beach's historic American Legion building. The American Legion, a significant cultural landmark serving the Black community, held particular importance to local residents and advocates.

State Representative Rob Long, who championed the American Legion funding, indicated he will not abandon the effort. He announced plans to advocate for the project again during next year's budget cycle. Despite the vetoes, Bernard characterized the overall outcome as favorable for the county, emphasizing that securing three-quarters of requested funding represents a successful budget year for Palm Beach County's infrastructure and community needs.

cards.headline: Two killed in Florida's Turnpike crash near Martin County mile marker 132, fifth traffic fatality in four days
cards.body:
A fatal crash on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County brought traffic to a standstill Monday afternoon, with both directions closed for several hours. The collision occurred near mile marker 132 around 3 p.m., according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The wreck claimed two lives and left another person with serious injuries who was transported to a hospital by ground ambulance.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office shut down all northbound and southbound lanes at 3:49 p.m. and warned the public to expect significant traffic delays lasting at least two to three hours. Officials urged drivers to seek alternate routes to avoid the area. All lanes have since reopened, though the exact cause of the crash remains undisclosed.

This deadly collision marks the fifth traffic fatality to occur in Martin County within a four-day span, highlighting a troubling surge in serious roadway incidents. Earlier Monday morning, a Palm City man died following a two-vehicle crash on the Turnpike. Just two days prior on Saturday morning, another fatal head-on collision claimed two lives on Allapattah Road in Indiantown.

The cluster of fatal crashes within such a short timeframe has raised concerns about road safety conditions in the Martin County area. As investigations continue into the cause of Monday's wreck, authorities remain focused on determining what factors contributed to the series of deadly incidents that have claimed multiple lives over the past several days.

cards.headline: One person dies in Monday afternoon house fire in Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: One person died Monday afternoon in a house fire in Hobe Sound, according to Martin County Fire Rescue.
cards.body:
One person died Monday afternoon in a house fire in Hobe Sound, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Firefighters responded just after 3 p.m. to a home in the 7000 block of Southeast Cactus Trail. When crews from Martin County Fire Rescue Station 32 arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from all doors and windows of the home. Firefighters entered the house, located an unresponsive person, and removed them from the home.

Paramedics treated the victim and transported them by ambulance to a hospital with life-threatening injuries. Martin County Fire Rescue later confirmed the person died. Stuart Fire Rescue also responded to assist under a mutual aid agreement. The State Fire Marshal has been notified and is investigating the cause of the fire.

cards.headline: DeSantis signs $117.6 billion Florida budget, vetoes $1.7 billion in spending
cards.teaser: Gov.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Florida's $117.6 billion budget, which takes effect July 1 and marks the start of the 2026-27 fiscal year. The budget includes a long-sought retirement benefit for Special Risk members of the Florida Retirement System, which encompasses most law enforcement and first-responder professions. Eligible retirees who have been retired for at least 5 years will receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment of at least 1.5%, marking the culmination of more than 15 years of advocacy by first responders and supporters in the Legislature. More than 125,000 first responders statewide are expected to benefit, including roughly 75,000 active Special Risk members enrolled in the Florida Retirement System.

The Sadowski Coalition, a bipartisan alliance of more than 40 statewide organizations, praised DeSantis for fully funding the state's two primary affordable housing programs. The budget sets aside $166 million for the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) and nearly $71 million for the State Apartment Incentive Loan (SAIL) program. SHIP provides funding to local governments for homeownership and housing assistance programs, while SAIL finances the construction and preservation of affordable rental housing throughout the state. Sadowski Coalition facilitator Mark Hendrickson said the investment will help families, seniors, veterans and working Floridians find affordable places to live.

cards.headline: Two killed in Florida's Turnpike crash near Palm City, fifth Martin County traffic fatality in four days
cards.teaser: Two people died Monday afternoon in a crash on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County that shut down all lanes in both directions for multiple hours.
cards.body:
A crash that killed two people on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County closed all lanes in both directions for multiple hours Monday afternoon. According to the Martin County Fire Rescue Facebook page, the wreck happened near mile marker 132 at about 3 p.m. In addition to the two fatalities, firefighter-paramedics transported one person with traumatic injuries by ground to the hospital. The Martin County Sheriff's Office posted at 3:49 p.m. that both northbound and southbound lanes were completely shut down, with officials warning drivers to expect traffic slowdowns for at least two to three hours. All lanes in both directions have since reopened.

The crash marks the fifth traffic fatality in four days in Martin County. A Palm City man died overnight following a two-vehicle crash on the Turnpike early Monday morning. Additionally, two people were killed in a head-on crash Saturday morning on Allapattah Road in Indiantown.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis signs $117.6 billion Florida budget with $1.6 billion in vetoes
cards.teaser: Gov.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Florida's $117.6 billion state budget Monday in Tampa, marking the fourth consecutive year the governor reduced spending through line-item vetoes. The budget takes effect July 1 and sets state priorities for the new fiscal year. DeSantis cut roughly $1.6 billion from the spending plan approved by lawmakers, with about $800 million tied to direct line-item spending. The vetoes included major reductions across corrections, water and resiliency projects, education, higher education, local public safety initiatives, and community programs. Some of the largest cuts hit Florida's prison system, including tens of millions of dollars tied to prison repairs, new correctional housing units, capital improvements, and pay adjustments. Water and resiliency projects saw more than $170 million in cuts, including local stormwater, wastewater, flood mitigation, and infrastructure projects across the state. Education cuts included $15 million for Catholic school security, along with millions more for college infrastructure and programs tied to Palm Beach State College, College of the Florida Keys, Indian River State College, and Florida State University's College of Nursing.

DeSantis framed the budget as an example of Florida's fiscal restraint, saying it still funds major priorities including education, transportation, environmental restoration, law enforcement, and tax relief. He pointed to roughly $18 billion in reserves and continued efforts to pay down state debt. House Minority Leader Fentrice Driskell criticized the vetoes, arguing Democratic projects were vetoed at a rate of roughly two to one compared to Republican counterparts. She questioned whether DeSantis was more focused on talking points about cutting the budget than on the people impacted by the cuts. DeSantis said this year's vetoes bring his budget cuts over eight years to more than $10 billion, far more than his recent predecessors combined.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce diver Greer Boyd, 63, identified after fatal dive near Fort Pierce Inlet
cards.teaser: Boyd went into the water alone to recover a trolling motor that had fallen overboard from his fishing boat Friday morning.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office identified Greer Boyd, 63, of Fort Pierce as the diver found dead Friday near the Fort Pierce Inlet. Boyd was fishing with friends earlier in the day when the boat's trolling motor became detached and went overboard. The group returned to the area with diving equipment to attempt to recover the motor.

Boyd went into the water alone, and only his buoyancy compensator and air tank were located approximately 40 yards from the boat. Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday regarding the missing diver. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed four vessels to assist in the search. Martin County Fire Rescue Lt. Daniel DeGrazia, who was off-duty at the time, assisted in the recovery and recovered Boyd's body at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. An autopsy was scheduled.

cards.headline: 400-pound black bear killed on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard
cards.teaser: The male black bear ran into the roadway Monday morning before being struck by a vehicle. The driver was not injured.
cards.body:
A 400-pound male black bear was killed Monday morning after being struck by a car on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Major Ruben Romero said the driver was not speeding and stopped to wait for deputies to arrive. The driver told deputies the bear ran into the roadway before being hit by the vehicle. The driver was not injured, but the bear died at the scene. Romero emphasized the importance of drivers being aware of wildlife, particularly on rural roads during morning and evening hours.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission removed the bear from the scene. Michael Orlando, bear program coordinator with FWC, said he believes the bear was dispersing, a period when bears leave their mother and pack to find a new home. According to Orlando, bears can walk 50 to 100 miles in any direction during this time. The bear is currently with FWC in Collier County, where officials will collect data to determine its origin. This marks the second bear sighting on the Treasure Coast this month, following a black bear spotted swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community of Port St. Lucie.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office posted at 3:49 p.m. that both northbound and southbound lanes were completely shut down, with traffic slowdowns expected for at least two to three hours. All lanes in both directions are now reopened. Drivers were urged to use alternate routes.

According to the sheriff's office, this is the fifth traffic fatality in four days in Martin County. A Palm City man died overnight after a two-vehicle crash on the Turnpike early Monday morning. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman, 78, killed after SUV rolls backward in residential driveway
cards.teaser: The 2016 Lincoln MKX began rolling backward Sunday morning, and the open driver's door struck the woman, knocking her to the ground.
cards.body:
A 78-year-old woman was killed Sunday morning after an SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway in Port St. Lucie, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The incident happened at approximately 10:47 a.m. when a 2016 Lincoln MKX SUV was parked in a residential driveway. The woman was standing outside the vehicle near the open driver's door when the SUV began rolling backward. The open door struck her, knocking her to the ground. Her adult son, 59, was in the passenger seat and had started the vehicle. The cause of the rollback remains under investigation.

The woman was rushed to Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, where she was pronounced deceased at 11:19 a.m. Neighbor Daisy Cardona witnessed the emergency response and spoke about the woman's kindness. "I saw the ambulance, the fire trucks, and two or three police cars. I felt sad, sad because I've known her for many years," Cardona said. "On Sundays, they would bring us bread, cupcakes, donuts, and sometimes cakes that were this big. May she rest in peace and my condolences to her family.

hero.headline: Singer Island development debate centers on Blue Heron Bridge reef
hero.teaser: A proposed 25-story waterfront development near Phil Foster Park on Singer Island is raising concerns about its impact on a world-renowned diving and snorkeling site.
hero.body:
A New York-based developer called The Continuum Company is proposing Singer Island Gateway, a roughly $14 million mixed-use project at 2525 Lake Drive in Palm Beach County. The development would include hundreds of residential units, commercial and public space, and a marina positioned near Blue Heron Bridge. A 25-story tower would mark the entrance to Singer Island at this location.

The area surrounding Phil Foster Park and the base of Blue Heron Bridge has become a destination for divers and snorkelers worldwide. Visitors to the reef describe encountering stingrays, colorful fish species, and coral formations in the shallow waters. The underwater ecosystem has gained recognition as one of the best diving spots for those who have explored it. The site offers visitors a unique marine environment that they say is unlike anywhere else they have experienced.

The proposed development has sparked concern among longtime residents about potential impacts on this delicate ecosystem. Gary Heiser, who grew up in the area, expressed significant doubts about whether such a large project fits the location. He said the 25-story tower would be out of scale with Singer Island and worried that construction activity, increased shade from the building, and the addition of a marina could disrupt the marine life below. "I find it hard to believe that there'd be no impact. I would like to see more research," Heiser said. However, not everyone shares this level of concern. Louis Espinosa, a visitor to the reef, said his position would depend on whether the project actually threatens the underwater environment. "If it doesn't disturb the reef, I don't see a problem with it," Espinosa said.

An environmental study published by the developer concludes that the planned development would have no negative impact on marine life in the Lake Worth Lagoon. A geoscientist involved in the study determined the ecosystem would remain unchanged. Despite this assessment, residents remain skeptical and have started a petition opposing the proposal. The developer has been contacted for additional comment. No approvals have been granted yet, and the project remains in the proposal stage as the community continues to debate its potential environmental consequences.

cards.teaser: First responders from Jupiter Fire Rescue, Delray Beach, and Palm Beach County fire departments have deployed to Venezuela as part of a FEMA Urban Search and Rescue Task Force.
cards.body:
First responders from Jupiter, Delray Beach, and Palm Beach County fire departments have deployed to Venezuela as part of a FEMA Urban Search and Rescue Task Force. Jupiter Fire Rescue said two of its firefighters are among a group of 80 deployed to the region. The crew was sent with less than 24 hours notice and is expected to remain in Venezuela for at least two weeks. The mission focuses on search and rescue operations in collapsed structures, ranging from large buildings to smaller homes.

The team brought heavy-duty equipment for breaking, cutting, breaching, and stabilization, as well as technical rope rescue tools. Stephen Shaw, deputy fire chief of operations for Jupiter Fire Rescue, said the deployment reflects the department's commitment to helping those in need. Shaw noted that the experience will strengthen the department when the crew returns home, as the learning and skills practiced will benefit Jupiter Fire Rescue internally as the department continues to grow.

cards.headline: 78-year-old woman killed after SUV rolls backward in Port St. Lucie driveway

A 78-year-old woman was killed Sunday morning after an SUV rolled backward in a residential driveway in Port St. Lucie, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The incident occurred at approximately 10:47 a.m. when a 2016 Lincoln MKX SUV began rolling backward while the woman was standing outside the vehicle near the open driver's door. The open door struck her and knocked her to the ground. Her adult son, 59, was in the passenger seat and had started the vehicle. The cause of the rollback remains under investigation.

The woman was transported to Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, where she was pronounced deceased at 11:19 a.m. Neighbor Daisy Cardona told WPTV that she witnessed emergency responders at the scene, including an ambulance, fire trucks, and two or three police cars. Cardona said she had known the woman for several years and remembered the family's regular acts of kindness. "On Sundays, they would bring us bread, cupcakes, donuts, and sometimes cakes," Cardona said. "May she rest in peace and my condolences to her family." The investigation remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Florida State Representative plans to push again for Delray Beach American Legion funding after veto
cards.teaser: A $200,000 request for repairs and operations at Delray Beach's historic American Legion building was vetoed by Governor Ron DeSantis. State Representative Rob Long said he plans to push again during next year's budget cycle.
cards.body:
State Representative Rob Long plans to push again for funding for Delray Beach's historic American Legion building after a $200,000 request for repairs and operations was vetoed by Governor Ron DeSantis in the state budget. Long told reporters he is not giving up and plans to push again during next year's budget cycle. The American Legion building is known as the area's historic Black hub, with residents citing its importance to the community. One resident recalled that her grandparents celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary in the building.

The veto was part of nearly $2 billion in spending proposals struck from the budget. Other Palm Beach County priorities that were vetoed included $2 million in expansions to parts of the county's water treatment plant, $900,000 for road improvements and beautification in South Bay, and $125,000 in improvements to the Ocean Inlet beach access. State Senator Mack Bernard noted that over $30 million was approved for Palm Beach County in the 2026-2027 budget, representing 75% of the funding requested.

cards.headline: Mighty Mussels defeat St. Lucie Mets 6-5 in weekend series finale
cards.teaser: The Fort Myers Mighty Mussels survived a late rally by the St. Lucie Mets to win 6-5 in their weekend series finale. The Mussels also had a game postponed and rescheduled for late July in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
The Fort Myers Mighty Mussels defeated the St. Lucie Mets 6-5 in their weekend series finale on Sunday, surviving a late rally by the Mets. Fragoza hit two home runs in the game for the Mussels.

Earlier in the weekend, a game between the Mussels and Mets was postponed. The game has been rescheduled for late July in Port St. Lucie. The teams compete in minor league baseball.

cards.headline: Messi scores in seventh straight World Cup game, extending record
cards.teaser: Lionel Messi became the first player to score in seven straight World Cup games while extending his goals record. The achievement came during weekend World Cup play.
cards.body:
Lionel Messi became the first player to score in seven straight World Cup games during weekend play, extending his World Cup goals record. The achievement marks another milestone in Messi's international career.

The World Cup is being played in 2026 with matches taking place across North America. Messi's scoring streak demonstrates continued form at the highest level of international competition.

cards.headline: Four candidates seek open Florida city council seat after incumbent declines to run
cards.teaser: Four candidates are seeking an open seat on a Florida city council after the incumbent announced they will not run for reelection. The election will fill the vacant position.
cards.body:
Four candidates are seeking an open seat on a Florida city council following an announcement that the incumbent will not run for reelection. The race will determine who fills the vacant position on the council.

The election represents an opportunity for new leadership on the council. The four candidates will compete to represent residents in the open seat race.

hero.headline: Boca Raton's George Snow Scholarship Fund Awards Record $7.5 Million to Local Students
hero.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund in Boca Raton awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026.
hero.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, has awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026, President Tim Snow told WPTV. The nonprofit has now distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students since its founding over 40 years ago, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County.

The program provides four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college, bridging the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford. Vice President of Development Jay Brandt noted that services go beyond financial help, providing mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast.

One 2026 recipient, Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship and plans to attend Georgetown University. The fund also operates the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, which offers professional, formal, and casual wear for scholars to use for interviews, internships, and campus life.

cards.headline: Vero Beach's MusicWorks Launches Fourteenth Concert Season
cards.body:
MusicWorks in Vero Beach is launching its fourteenth concert season, expanding cultural tourism and inspiring travel from multiple states including California, Texas, New York, Tennessee, Georgia, Illinois, Nevada, Arizona, Michigan and Massachusetts. The organization's season launch positions Florida alongside these ten states in a multi-state cultural initiative.

The concert series in Vero Beach has grown to attract visitors from across the country over its fourteen-year history. The new season represents continued expansion of the local cultural venue's reach beyond Florida's borders.

MusicWorks has established Vero Beach as a destination for concert tourism, drawing audiences willing to travel significant distances for performances. The alignment with major states like California, New York and Texas reflects the organization's national profile.

The fourteenth season continues MusicWorks' role in bringing professional concert performances to Indian River County. Specific concert dates and performers for the new season were not detailed in the announcement.

hero.headline: Florida restores cost-of-living adjustments for retired first responders starting July 1
hero.teaser: More than 125,000 first responders statewide will benefit from restored retirement benefits after a 15-year advocacy campaign.
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a $117.6 billion state budget that brings back annual cost-of-living adjustments for retired firefighters, paramedics and law enforcement officers beginning July 1. The restoration of this benefit represents a significant victory after more than 15 years of advocacy efforts by first responders and their legislative supporters. Eligible retirees who have been retired for at least five years will receive an annual COLA of at least 1.5 percent under the new plan.

The policy affects Special Risk members of the Florida Retirement System, a category that includes most law enforcement and first-responder professions across the state. More than 125,000 first responders statewide are expected to benefit from this change, including approximately 75,000 active Special Risk members currently enrolled in the Florida Retirement System. The restoration addresses concerns that retirees have struggled to maintain their purchasing power as inflation has eroded their fixed incomes over time.

Florida Professional Firefighters President Wayne "Bernie" Bernoska emphasized that the restored benefit acknowledges the dedication of the state's first responders. "Restoring the cost-of-living adjustment strengthens that commitment while recognizing the sacrifices made by Florida's firefighters, paramedics and law enforcement officers throughout their careers," Bernoska said. He also noted that the change reinforces the state's commitment to valuing public safety professionals both during and after their service. Beyond immediate financial relief, supporters argue the adjustment will strengthen recruitment and retention efforts across fire departments, law enforcement agencies and other public safety organizations.

Several lawmakers played crucial roles in achieving this outcome. Senator Joe Gruters was among the earliest champions of the cause, while Senate Budget Chief Ed Hooper, himself a former firefighter, helped guide the legislation through the legislative process. Other supporting lawmakers receiving recognition from the Florida Professional Firefighters include Senators Demi Busatta, Danny Alvarez and Omar Blanco, as well as the late Representative Joe Casello, a former Massachusetts firefighter who served in the Florida House representing South Florida. The combination of sustained advocacy and bipartisan legislative support ultimately resulted in the inclusion of this long-sought benefit in the state's budget.

cards.headline: DeSantis signs $117.6 billion Florida budget, vetoes $1.7 billion in spending
cards.teaser: Gov.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Florida's $117.6 billion budget, which takes effect July 1 and marks the start of the 2026-27 fiscal year. The budget includes a long-sought retirement benefit for Special Risk members of the Florida Retirement System, which encompasses most law enforcement and first-responder professions. Eligible retirees who have been retired for at least 5 years will receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment of at least 1.5%, marking the culmination of more than 15 years of advocacy by first responders and supporters in the Legislature. More than 125,000 first responders statewide are expected to benefit, including roughly 75,000 active Special Risk members enrolled in the Florida Retirement System.

The Sadowski Coalition, a bipartisan alliance of more than 40 statewide organizations, praised DeSantis for fully funding the state's two primary affordable housing programs. The budget sets aside $166 million for the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) and nearly $71 million for the State Apartment Incentive Loan (SAIL) program. SHIP provides funding to local governments for homeownership and housing assistance programs, while SAIL finances the construction and preservation of affordable rental housing throughout the state. Sadowski Coalition facilitator Mark Hendrickson said the investment will help families, seniors, veterans and working Floridians find affordable places to live.

cards.headline: Florida budget projects tied to campaign donors and lobbyists survive DeSantis veto pen
cards.teaser: While DeSantis cut $1.7 billion in spending, millions in narrowly drawn budget items connected to contributors remained untouched.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis vetoed roughly $810 million in line items and $1.7 billion overall from the state budget, but a review of his veto transmittal letter reveals a long list of narrowly drawn projects connected to campaign contributors and lobbyists that survived untouched. The budget includes $6 million for the Florida Department of Law Enforcement to expand statewide use of a criminal-intelligence platform built by Peregrine Technologies, a data-integration firm that raised $250 million in June at a valuation near $6.8 billion. The platform stitches together dozens of siloed police, court and jail databases into a single searchable system.

The budget also steers money to several other connected entities. It provides $4 million for hearing-protection equipment for police officers from Starkey, the hearing-technology company founded by Minnesota billionaire Bill Austin, marking the third straight budget to fund Starkey products. Austin gave $50,000 to House Speaker Danny Perez's political committee the day before the Legislative Session convened. The budget includes $4 million for a gasification project led by ReaSYN Technologies, a Miami startup incorporated in June 2024 that donated $100,000 apiece to political committees controlled by DeSantis and Perez, and $150,000 to one backing Senate President Ben Albritton. The company had already collected about $5 million in earlier state support for a pilot at a Putnam County landfill.

cards.headline: DeSantis vetoes naturopathic doctor licensing bill after Legislature passage
cards.teaser: The governor said Florida law already allows licensed healthcare professionals to incorporate naturopathic methods into their practices.
cards.body:
Legislation that would have established a licensure pathway for naturopathic doctors in Florida died after Governor DeSantis vetoed the measure Friday. SB 688 would have created a Board of Naturopathic Medicine within the Department of Health, established licensing standards for naturopathic doctors and authorized them to diagnose and treat patients using natural therapies while prohibiting surgery, prescription drugs other than certain natural substances and procedures outside the profession's scope.

The proposal advanced through the Legislature despite opposition from physicians and consumer advocates, who argued it would give naturopathic doctors overly broad authority to diagnose and treat disease. Sen. Ana Maria Rodriguez disputed those critiques and emphasized that the measure would not have allowed naturopathic doctors to perform surgery or treat cancer, and would have limited their prescribing authority to natural herbs and nutritional supplements. In his veto message, DeSantis said Florida law already allows licensed healthcare professionals to incorporate naturopathic methods into their practices and argued the bill would create unnecessary bureaucracy. He also noted there are no barriers to accessing natural remedies, as they do not require a prescription or FDA approval. The Governor further argued the proposal could disadvantage practitioners by requiring postgraduate education not currently available in Florida and by adding new licensing fees.

cards.headline: DeSantis signs expansion of Veterans Dental Care Grant Program
cards.teaser: The program will provide oral healthcare to veterans with incomes up to 400 percent of the federal poverty level starting July 1.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed legislation expanding the Veterans Dental Care Grant Program, housed within the Florida Department of Veterans' Affairs. HB 253 broadens the program to provide oral healthcare to veterans with incomes up to 400 percent of the federal poverty level. Rep. Jervonte Edmonds sponsored the measure in the House, while Sen. Shevrin Jones carried it in the Senate.

According to the lawmakers, research consistently shows a strong connection between oral health and overall physical well-being. The grant program will expand access to preventive and restorative dental care for eligible veterans who may otherwise struggle to obtain treatment. "Dental care is healthcare. Our veterans have sacrificed for our country, and they deserve access to the care that allows them to live healthier, more confident lives," Edmonds said. The new law takes effect July 1.

cards.headline: House passes Rep. Laurel Lee's legislation to strengthen power grid cybersecurity
cards.teaser: The Energy Emergency Leadership Act will establish clear leadership within the Department of Energy during energy emergencies.
cards.body:
The House has passed Republican U.S. Rep. Laurel Lee's Energy Emergency Leadership Act (HR 7258) to strengthen and secure the U.S. electric grid. The bipartisan bill passed on a voice vote, months after Lee carried the bill through the Energy and Commerce Committee. The legislation requires a Senate-confirmed leader to direct the Office of Cyber Security, Energy Security, and Emergency Response.

Lee said the Energy Emergency Leadership Act strengthens the nation's ability to prepare for and respond to threats to the electric grid by establishing clear leadership and accountability within the Department of Energy during energy emergencies. She emphasized that as cyber threats against critical energy infrastructure continue to grow, the federal government must be prepared to respond quickly and effectively. Lee noted that leadership is especially important for Florida, where hurricanes and other severe weather events regularly test the resilience of energy infrastructure. U.S. Rep. Kathy Castor, a Tampa Democrat, also touted the legislation's importance, noting that as the grid becomes increasingly complex and faces new challenges, ensuring grid security must be managed by top officials. The legislation will now head to the Senate for consideration. Should it pass, the bill will go to President Donald Trump's desk for his signature.

cards.headline: Florida unemployment rate levels at 4.8 percent in May after months of increases
cards.teaser: The state's unemployment rate had increased every other month this year before stabilizing last month.
cards.body:
Florida's unemployment rate leveled out at 4.8 percent in May after increasing every other month this year, according to the latest numbers released last week. The same day Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the $117.6 billion state budget and vetoed about $1.7 billion in spending, House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell held a press conference criticizing the governor's priorities. Driskell said Democrats were disproportionately targeted in the vetoes at a rate of 2-to-1 and that cuts affected projects supporting veterans, children with autism, youth support programs, opioid and drug abuse prevention programs, seniors, and pregnant mothers.

Driskell argued DeSantis should have invested more heavily in affordable housing and job training given the unemployment figures. She said people are struggling to pay their bills and that under DeSantis's administration, billions of taxpayer dollars have been squandered on schemes like Alligator Alcatraz, the Hope Florida scandal, debt prescription drug importation programs, and renaming airports. "None of these things help put food on the table or help people put gas in their tanks," the Tampa Democrat said. Driskell also criticized DeSantis for using his veto pen in a partisan manner, calling it "the partisan underbelly of politics that people hate."

hero.headline: 400-pound black bear killed in Martin County traffic accident
hero.teaser: A 400-pound black bear was killed in a traffic accident in Martin County. Wildlife officials say bear sightings are uncommon in the area.
hero.body:
A 400-pound black bear was struck and killed in a traffic accident in Martin County, according to wildlife officials quoted in local reports.

The incident occurred as Martin County experienced a significant spike in traffic fatalities. The same week saw at least five fatal crashes across the county within a four-day period. On Monday alone, a double fatal crash closed all lanes of Florida's Turnpike in both directions near mile marker 132 around 3 p.m. The wreck killed two people and sent a third person with traumatic injuries to the hospital. The closure lasted several hours, and authorities urged drivers to seek alternate routes while warning of potential delays lasting two to three hours.

Earlier that same Monday morning, a Palm City resident died in a separate two-vehicle crash on the Turnpike. Additionally, a head-on collision on Allapattah Road in Indiantown on Saturday morning claimed two more lives. The string of fatal accidents underscored dangerous driving conditions throughout the county during that period.

Wildlife officials noted that bear sightings remain uncommon in Martin County, making the fatal traffic accident noteworthy for local wildlife monitoring. The circumstances surrounding the bear's presence on a roadway and the specific details of the collision were not detailed in available reports. Authorities indicated they are continuing to monitor the situation as wildlife encounters in the area remain relatively rare events.

cards.headline: Two killed in Florida's Turnpike crash near Palm City, fifth Martin County traffic fatality in four days

cards.body:
A crash that killed two people on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County closed all lanes in both directions for multiple hours Monday afternoon. According to the Martin County Fire Rescue Facebook page, the wreck happened near mile marker 132 at about 3 p.m. In addition to the two fatalities, firefighter-paramedics transported one person with traumatic injuries by ground to the hospital. The Martin County Sheriff's Office posted at 3:49 p.m. that both northbound and southbound lanes were completely shut down, with officials warning drivers to expect traffic slowdowns for at least two to three hours. All lanes in both directions have since reopened.

The crash marks the fifth traffic fatality in four days in Martin County. A Palm City man died overnight following a two-vehicle crash on the Turnpike early Monday morning. Additionally, two people were killed in a head-on crash Saturday morning on Allapattah Road in Indiantown.

cards.headline: Palm City man dies in early Monday Turnpike crash
cards.teaser: A Palm City man died overnight in a two-vehicle crash on Florida's Turnpike early Monday morning. The crash was one of five fatal traffic incidents in Martin County over four days.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce diver identified after fatal accident near Fort Pierce Inlet
cards.teaser: The St.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has identified Greer Boyd, 63, of Fort Pierce as the diver found dead on Friday near the Fort Pierce Inlet. Investigators say Boyd was fishing with friends earlier in the day when the boat's trolling motor became detached and went overboard. The group returned to the area with diving equipment to recover the motor. Boyd went into the water alone, and only his buoyancy compensator and air tank were located approximately 40 yards from the boat.

Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday regarding a missing diver. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed four vessels to assist in the search. Martin County Fire Rescue Lt. Daniel DeGrazia was off-duty at the time and assisted in the recovery effort. DeGrazia recovered Boyd's body at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. An autopsy is scheduled today.

hero.headline: 25-Story Singer Island Gateway Development Raises Concerns Over World-Renowned Blue Heron Bridge Reef
hero.body:
A proposed 25-story waterfront development on Singer Island is generating debate about potential impacts to one of the region's most celebrated diving destinations. The Continuum Company, a New York-based developer, has unveiled plans for Singer Island Gateway, a roughly $14 million mixed-use project located at 2525 Lake Drive. The development would feature hundreds of residential units, commercial space, public areas, and a marina positioned near the base of Blue Heron Bridge in Palm Beach County.

The shallow waters surrounding Phil Foster Park at Blue Heron Bridge have become a global attraction for divers and snorkelers seeking to experience a distinctive underwater environment. Visitors to the reef encounter a diverse array of marine life, including stingrays, rainbow-colored fish, blue and yellow fish, pink and yellow coral, and striped species. The unique ecosystem has earned the location recognition as one of the best diving spots available, drawing enthusiasts from around the world who describe the underwater world as beautiful and amazing.

Longtime resident Gary Heiser has emerged as a vocal critic of the project, questioning whether a structure of this scale fits the location. He expressed concern that construction activities, shade cast by the 25-story tower, and the addition of a marina could harm the marine life that has made the reef renowned internationally. An environmental study published by the developer, conducted by a geoscientist, concluded that the development would have no impact on marine life in the Lake Worth Lagoon and that the ecosystem would remain unchanged. However, Heiser remains skeptical of these findings, calling for additional research to verify the conclusions.

Opinions among reef visitors vary on the proposal. While Espinosa acknowledged the reef as one of the best spots he has visited, he indicated his position would depend on whether the development actually threatens the underwater environment. He stated, "If it doesn't disturb the reef, I don't see a problem with it." The project has not yet received approval from local authorities. The developer has been contacted for additional comment, though a response remains pending. Community opposition has materialized in the form of a resident petition against the proposal, indicating significant local concern about the development's potential consequences for this cherished natural resource.

cards.headline: Palm City Man Dies in Crash Between SUV and Semi-Truck on Florida's Turnpike
cards.teaser: A 41-year-old Palm City man died early Monday morning after his Nissan Rogue collided with a semi-truck trailer on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County.
cards.body: A 41-year-old Palm City man died early Monday morning after his Nissan Rogue SUV collided with a semi-truck on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County at mile marker 136. According to Florida Highway Patrol, the Nissan was traveling northbound in the outside lane when it struck the back of the semi-truck's trailer, also in the outside lane. The driver was transported to Florida Coast Medical Center and pronounced deceased at 1:55 a.m. The semi-truck driver was not injured. FHP is investigating the crash.

cards.headline: Diver Found Dead Near Fort Pierce Inlet Identified as 63-Year-Old Fort Pierce Man
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office identified Greer Boyd, 63, of Fort Pierce as the diver found dead Friday while attempting to recover a trolling motor near the Fort Pierce Inlet.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has identified the diver found dead on Friday near the Fort Pierce Inlet as Greer Boyd, 63, of Fort Pierce. Investigators say Boyd was fishing with friends earlier in the day when the boat's trolling motor became detached and went overboard. The group returned to the area with diving equipment in an attempt to recover the motor. Boyd went into the water alone, and only his buoyancy compensator and air tank were located approximately 40 yards from the boat.

Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday regarding a missing diver. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed four vessels to assist in the search. Martin County Fire Rescue Lt. Daniel DeGrazia, who was off-duty at the time, assisted in the recovery effort. DeGrazia recovered Boyd's body at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. An autopsy is scheduled today.

cards.headline: 400-Pound Black Bear Killed by Car on Southwest Martin Highway in Martin County
cards.teaser: A 400-pound male black bear was killed Monday morning after being hit by a car on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard in Martin County.
cards.body:
A 400-pound male black bear was killed Monday morning after being hit by a car on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Major Ruben Romero said the driver was not speeding and stopped to wait for deputies to arrive. The driver reported that the bear ran into the roadway before being struck. The driver was not injured, but the bear died at the scene. Romero emphasized the importance of driver awareness regarding wildlife, particularly on rural roads during morning and evening hours.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission removed the bear from the scene. Michael Orlando, the FWC's bear program coordinator, believes the bear was dispersing, a stage when bears leave their mother and pack to find a new home. Orlando noted that bears can walk 50 to 100 miles in any direction during this period. The bear is currently with FWC in Collier County, where officials will collect data to determine its origin. This marks the second bear sighting on the Treasure Coast this month, following a black bear caught on camera swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community of Port St. Lucie.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Flights Starting at $41 in July
cards.teaser: Flights from Vero Beach Regional Airport will start at $41 in July, according to published reports.
cards.body: Cheap Florida flights at Vero Beach Regional Airport, identified by the airport code VRB, start at $41 in July, according to Treasure Coast News. The low fares represent options for travelers departing from the Vero Beach area next month. No additional details about specific routes or carriers were provided in the report.
